clue.text: Hose the vessel thoroughly, it may be infested with small burrowing creatures

definitions.text: it may be infested with small burrowing creatures

parts.note: to hose something is to water it
a ship is a sea-going vessel
down as in 'hose down', meaning wash completely

explanation.surface: An instruction to give a boat a good sluicing, as if it were overrun with vermin.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Adams's novel is named after a real Hampshire hill, home to its rabbits; the definition describes that down rather than the book.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional hill in Adams's novel is a warren full of rabbits, burrowing animals.

clue.text: This lucky spinner perhaps predictably foreshadowed scandalous risks and ultimate prizes (, 7)

definitions.meaning: a gambling device that spins to decide prizes, or the turning wheel of chance in myth

definitions.text: foreshadowed scandalous risks and ultimate prizes
definitions.meaning: Susan Howatch's earlier novel came before her Starbridge books Scandalous Risks and Ultimate Prizes

explanation.walkthrough: Scandalous Risks and Ultimate Prizes are titles of Susan Howatch novels; her 1984 saga came before them.
explanation.definitionFit: A spun wheel deciding luck is the classic image of chance, and it is also the title of a Howatch family saga.

clue.text: Tragic heroine from wild coast

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of the next word running out of control into a new order

explanation.surface: A doomed heroine emerging from a rugged stretch of shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges COAST.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's opera heroine leaps to her death, a classic tragic figure.

clue.text: Chaucerian stanza necessitating loyal toil, perhaps

definitions.text: Chaucerian stanza necessitating loyal toil, perhaps

parts.words: Chaucerian stanza necessitating loyal toil, perhaps
parts.note: a seven-line verse form used by Chaucer, whose name suggests words chiming with loyal and toil, as a kingly sort of sound match

explanation.surface: A medieval verse form that demands faithful hard labour of the poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The stanza's second word chimes with 'loyal' (and roughly with 'toil'), so its name describes the matching sounds it demands.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer used this seven-line pentameter stanza in Troilus and Criseyde.

clue.text: According to Frank McKinney "Kin" Hubbard, nobody forgets where he buried it

definitions.text: According to Frank McKinney "Kin" Hubbard, nobody forgets where he buried it

parts.words: According to Frank McKinney "Kin" Hubbard, nobody forgets where he buried it
parts.note: the American humorist's quip that people never forget where they buried a quarrel's weapon, i.e. a grudge is never truly dropped

explanation.surface: A quotation from an American humorist about buried things.
explanation.walkthrough: Hubbard twists the idiom 'bury the hatchet' (make peace): the quarrel is only ever buried where it can be dug up again.
explanation.definitionFit: Burying a small axe is the idiom for ending a quarrel, which Hubbard says is never really forgotten.

clue.text: English historian of Scotland? sounds like a quiet revolutionary

indicators.note: signals that the answer is spoken the same as the words that follow

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, quiet; a rebel is a revolutionary

explanation.surface: Asks whether a chronicler of Scottish history is really a mild-mannered insurgent.
explanation.walkthrough: P (quiet) followed by REBEL is said the same as the historian's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: John Prebble was an English writer best known for histories such as Culloden and The Highland Clearances.

clue.text: "By all the operation of the / From whom we do exist…" (King Lear)

definitions.text: "By all the operation of the / From whom we do exist…" (King Lear)

parts.words: "By all the operation of the / From whom we do exist…" (King Lear)
parts.note: Lear swears by the heavenly bodies whose influence governs life; the missing word fills the gap in the quotation

explanation.surface: A line from King Lear with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear disowns Cordelia swearing by the planets and stars, thought to govern human fate.
explanation.definitionFit: The heavenly spheres were believed to rule existence, hence Lear's oath by them.

clue.text: Direction taken by two twentieth-century American writers

parts.note: Sterling North wrote Rascal
Nathanael West wrote Miss Lonelyhearts

explanation.surface: A course followed by a pair of modern American authors.
explanation.definitionFit: A compass bearing between two cardinal points is a direction.

clue.text: Normal shops hit badly by Dickensian creation

indicators.note: badly tells us the letters of the three words before it are knocked out of their usual order

explanation.surface: Ordinary stores suffering at the hands of a character from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit' looks like the verb of the surface but is fodder; 'badly' rearranges NORMALSHOPSHIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Plornish, the plasterer of Bleeding Heart Yard, is a character in Little Dorrit.

clue.text: A small slice of lamb, say

definitions.text: A small slice of lamb, say

parts.words: A small slice of lamb, say
parts.note: Charles Lamb wrote short prose pieces, so a little bit of Lamb's writing is a brief composition

explanation.surface: A modest cut of meat from a young sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb is Charles Lamb, author of the Essays of Elia, not the meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A diminutive composition, the sort of short piece Charles Lamb was famous for.

clue.text: American novelist in hot pursuit of a Simpson

indicators.note: one piece chasing another means it comes after it

parts.note: Bart is a son in the cartoon family The Simpsons
H is the abbreviation for hot on taps

explanation.surface: A US author chasing a cartoon character hard.
explanation.definitionFit: John Barth is a US writer of novels such as The Sot-Weed Factor.

clue.text: Mortimer's seemed to belong to a mathematician

definitions.text: Mortimer's seemed to belong to a mathematician

parts.words: Mortimer's seemed to belong to a mathematician
parts.note: John Mortimer's novel title Summer's ... reads as if the agreement were owned by someone who adds up figures

explanation.surface: Something of Mortimer's looked as if it were owned by a numbers person.
explanation.walkthrough: John Mortimer wrote Summer's Lease; a summer read as 'one who sums' is a mathematician.
explanation.definitionFit: A rental contract, the word completing Mortimer's novel title after Summer's.

clue.text: Goddess in the best tradition

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A deity shown in the finest light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the run inside 'the best'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebe is the Greek deity of youth, cupbearer to the Olympians.

clue.text: Examine tangled netting to reveal flood survivor

annotationWithheld.why: Examine tangled netting to reveal flood survivor (4): the only parse is an indirect anagram (netting = MESH, tangled to SHEM), a synonym scrambled, which the check refuses; 'Examine' is otherwise unexplained
annotationWithheld.clue: Examine tangled netting to reveal flood survivor

clue.text: Such a rudimentary literary form isn't worth peanuts (, )

definitions.text: Such a rudimentary literary form isn't worth peanuts

parts.words: Such a rudimentary literary form isn't worth peanuts
parts.note: Peanuts is Schulz's cartoon series, so the humble form it belongs to is worth exactly that

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark that a basic kind of writing is valueless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'isn't worth peanuts' sounds like scorn, but Peanuts is Charles Schulz's cartoon, an example of the form.
explanation.definitionFit: Peanuts is a famous newspaper cartoon series of panels.

clue.text: A sort of cinematic curtain exploited by H. G. Wells's Man

definitions.text: A sort of cinematic curtain exploited by H. G. Wells's Man

parts.words: A sort of cinematic curtain exploited by H. G. Wells's Man
parts.note: a film's gradual dimming to black, which is also how Wells's unseen hero vanishes from view

explanation.surface: A film-closing device used by the Invisible Man.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells's Invisible Man disappears gradually, just as a film scene dims away.
explanation.definitionFit: A gradual dimming of the picture to end a film scene, which the Invisible Man performs on himself.

clue.text: Medical man (university doctor, American Medical Association), produces television play based on facts

parts.note: doc is informal for a physician
AMA is its initials

explanation.surface: A medic with university and professional credentials makes a factual TV play.
explanation.definitionFit: A dramatised factual programme blends documentary and drama.

clue.text: Poems of great sweep (see Pope's comeback)

indicators.note: a comeback turns the run of words back on itself so it is read from the end

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the 's giving no letter; whole words are turned, so the run reading backwards across them is the setter's design, not a coincidence

explanation.surface: Epic poems, with a cross-reference to the poet Pope's return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comeback' turns SEEPOPE round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Epic poems are grand in scale and sweep.

clue.text: Tough hanger-on for Tolkien creature in Chekhov setting

indicators.note: a hanger-on trails behind, so the tough word is attached after the creature

parts.note: orcs are goblin soldiers in The Lord of the Rings
hard means tough

explanation.surface: A strong follower of a Middle-earth monster in a Russian play.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cherry Orchard is the setting and title of Chekhov's last play.

clue.text: "The horrid Woe drips from the hands" (Dylan Thomas)

definitions.text: "The horrid Woe drips from the hands" (Dylan Thomas)

parts.words: "The horrid Woe drips from the hands" (Dylan Thomas)
parts.note: a line from Dylan Thomas with a word missing before hands, a kitchen cloth image

explanation.surface: A line of Dylan Thomas verse with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word describes hands as limp and wet as a kitchen cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloth for washing up crockery, which fills the gap in Thomas's line.

clue.text: "There were three sailors of City" (Tennyson)

parts.note: the opening line of the comic ballad Little Billee, with the name of a West Country port missing

explanation.surface: A ballad line about three seamen from a city, with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line actually comes from Thackeray's ballad Little Billee; the missing word is an English port city in the West Country.
explanation.definitionFit: A port city on the Avon in south-west England, home of the three sailors in the ballad.

clue.text: Club employee like Milnean wild beast?

definitions.meaning: a doorman who ejects troublemakers from a nightclub
Tigger in Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh stories is always springing about, so he is one who springs

explanation.walkthrough: Tigger, the tiger in A. A. Milne's Pooh stories, is famous for bouncing.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightclub door guard ejects people, and Milne's Tigger springs everywhere.

clue.text: A regular influence on some 10 tales?

definitions.text: A regular influence on some 10 tales?

parts.words: A regular influence on some 10 tales?
parts.note: 10 across is the novelist Barth, whose book The ... Tales opens with this word; the sea's twice-daily rise and fall is a regular influence

explanation.surface: Wonders what steadily shapes certain stories.
explanation.walkthrough: John Barth (10 across) wrote The Tidewater Tales; the sea's twice-daily rise and fall is the regular influence.
explanation.definitionFit: The rise and fall of the sea comes at regular intervals, governed by the moon.

clue.text: Hairy hunter from Charlemagne's Austrian territory

indicators.note: from tells us the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A shaggy huntsman coming out of the Frankish emperor's Austrian lands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' takes the run across 'Charlemagne's Austrian'; 'territory' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Jacob's brother is a hairy man and a skilful hunter.

clue.text: German composer starts symphonic poem (only half realized)

indicators.note: starts points to the opening letters of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A German composer begins a tone poem that is left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' takes the first letters of symphonic, poem, only, half, realized.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Spohr was a German Romantic violinist and composer.

clue.text: Kimball, an orphan

parts.note: Kipling's boy hero Kim is an orphaned son of an Irish soldier, and Kimball is his full first name

explanation.surface: A name and status, as if from a register.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Kim's full name is Kimball O'Hara.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Kipling's orphan hero Kim, whose first name is Kimball.

clue.text: She's out of danger, having no Latin

definitions.note: the 's is a link, is, so the definition is she, a female being

indicators.note: having no means the letter for Latin is taken away

parts.note: peril means danger

explanation.surface: A woman safe from harm who never learnt Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: A Persian fairy or sprite, always female, as in Gilbert and Sullivan's Iolanthe.

clue.text: Newcastle Brown for hymnodist?

parts.note: NE is the postcode for Newcastle upon Tyne
brown ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: Asks whether the famous Tyneside beer could stand for a hymn writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Newcastle Brown Ale is a well-known beer from north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: John Mason Neale wrote and translated hymns such as Good King Wenceslas.

clue.text: Carrier in charge shortly gets sorted out: produces complex musical items

indicators.note: sorted out means the letters are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: I/C is the short form of in charge

explanation.surface: A carrier in command gets organised and turns out intricate music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorted out' rearranges CARRIER plus IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Ricercari are elaborate contrapuntal instrumental compositions, forerunners of the fugue.

clue.text: Greater effect when trying to caused by David Hockney

definitions.meaning: a larger impact when trying to make a splash
Hockney's 1967 painting of a swimming pool, the white burst left by a diver

explanation.walkthrough: The first definition completes 'trying to make a splash'; the second is Hockney's famous swimming-pool painting.
explanation.definitionFit: A more dramatic impact, and the title of Hockney's pool painting.
